candidateArtifact.completeText:
# LUMINAiRY profile candidate

Name: Hannah Fry
Role: Keeper of the Explanation

About: Fry’s contribution is making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question. In Hello World, she asks who should decide a criminal case: a person or an algorithm. The point is not that one is automatically fairer. Each can fail differently, and those differences matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices. Cambridge recognized her public communication with the 2026 Leelavati Prize. LAiDIES calls her Keeper of the Explanation because she turns a hidden system into questions a reader can use: What is it optimizing? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?

Lesson: Make an invisible technical system understandable by showing where it touches ordinary decisions.

Image: /assets/mavens/y2k-stained-glass-v4-dark-sapphire/hannah-fry-y2k-stained-glass.png

Resources (preserved exactly):
- read: Read Cambridge profile — https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/person/hf418
- watch: Watch AI Confidential — https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002q76d/ai-confidential-with-hannah-fry-series-1-1-the-boy-who-tried-to-kill-the-queen
- listen: Listen to The Rest Is Science — https://therestis.com/science
- listen: Listen to Google DeepMind: The Podcast — https://deepmind.google/the-podcast/
- watch: Watch Hannah Fry on YouTube — https://www.youtube.com/@fryrsquared
- follow: Follow Hannah Fry on Instagram — https://www.instagram.com/fryrsquared/
- follow: Follow Hannah Fry on X — https://x.com/FryRsquared

Freshness: Role and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026

reverseBrief.humanQuestion: Why does LAiDIES celebrate Hannah Fry — what does she actually give an adult beginner beyond a Cambridge title?
reverseBrief.promisedPayoff: The reader learns that Fry makes the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question, and leaves with three reusable questions to ask of any consequential system.
reverseBrief.distinctiveContribution: Making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question — not merely popularizing math, but converting hidden systems into questions a non-expert can use.
reverseBrief.concreteExample: Hello World's opening dilemma: accused of a crime, who should decide your fate — a person or an algorithm? Neither is automatically fairer; each fails differently.
reverseBrief.readerConsequence: These differing failure modes matter when systems shape healthcare, justice, or other consequential choices in the reader's own life; the reader carries the consequence.
reverseBrief.usefulEntryPoint: Three portable questions — What is it optimizing? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence? — plus seven preserved links (book context via Cambridge profile, AI Confidential, two podcasts, YouTube, socials).

incumbentControl.reason: The incumbent About — 'Cambridge lists Fry as Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics.' — is title-only biography. It supplies no distinctive contribution, no concrete example, no reader consequence, and no entry point; it tells an adult beginner what Fry is called, not why she matters. Independently judged; it does not inherit the candidate's verdict.

plainClarity.reason: Every sentence is plain, short, and jargon-free; 'optimizing' is the hardest word and is immediately grounded by the parallel questions. No glossary accumulation, no mechanism-before-motivation.
plainClarity.artifactExcerpt: The point is not that one is automatically fairer. Each can fail differently, and those differences matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices.

distinctiveContribution.reason: The first sentence names a specific, differentiating contribution — visibility of the math inside automated decisions for ordinary questioners — corroborated by the Leelavati citation's language about translating mathematics for the public with originality. It is not an award list or a title restatement.
distinctiveContribution.artifactExcerpt: Fry’s contribution is making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.

concreteExample.reason: One vivid, verifiable example from Hello World does real work: it dramatizes the contribution rather than decorating it, and it matches Penguin's own framing of the book's opening question.
concreteExample.artifactExcerpt: In Hello World, she asks who should decide a criminal case: a person or an algorithm.

readerConsequence.reason: The consequence lands on the reader's own life — systems in healthcare and justice — and the final question explicitly assigns the stakes to the reader: who carries the consequence.
readerConsequence.artifactExcerpt: those differences matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices

usefulEntryPoint.reason: The three closing questions are a genuinely portable tool a beginner can apply the same day, and the seven preserved links give graded ways in (read, watch, listen, follow). The ending is a usable instrument, not a generic inspirational flourish.
usefulEntryPoint.artifactExcerpt: questions a reader can use: What is it optimizing? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence?

surfaceFit.reason: The About is exactly 100 words, a single paragraph, structured contribution → example → consequence → tool; it fits a shared card without cramping, and all card fields (role, lesson, image, links, freshness) sit in their expected slots.
surfaceFit.artifactExcerpt: Lesson: Make an invisible technical system understandable by showing where it touches ordinary decisions.

voice.reason: Third-person, warm-factual, no first-person founder voice, no jargon, no template repetition, and the LAiDIES framing is attributed rather than asserted as fact ('LAiDIES calls her...'). Ends on working questions, not a platitude.
voice.artifactExcerpt: LAiDIES calls her Keeper of the Explanation because she turns a hidden system into questions a reader can use

lockedFieldPreservation.reason: I compared the artifact text against the successor profile: name, role, lesson, image path, all seven links (types, labels, URLs, order) and the freshness line are byte-identical to the locked values; only 'about' changed, matching the change proof.
lockedFieldPreservation.artifactExcerpt: Freshness: Role and destinations checked 2 Sep 2026

facts.reason: Penguin's page for Hello World opens with precisely this dilemma; the artifact reports it accurately as a question the book asks.
facts.artifactExcerpt: In Hello World, she asks who should decide a criminal case: a person or an algorithm.
facts.sourceExcerpt: You are accused of a crime. Who would you rather determined your fate – a human or an algorithm?

facts.reason: Penguin's copy supports the book's scope (healthcare, justice among decision domains) and that it 'exposes their limitations' — but this is publisher promotional copy, not independent judgment of the book, so the claim is supported only within that limit. The artifact wisely avoids Penguin's stronger promotional claim that algorithms are 'less prone to error.'
facts.artifactExcerpt: Each can fail differently, and those differences matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices.
facts.sourceExcerpt: making important decisions – in healthcare, transport, finance, security, what we watch, where we go even who we send to prison ... she lifts the lid on their inner workings, demonstrates their power, exposes their limitations

facts.reason: The prize, the year context, and its public-communication basis are supported, but the awarding attribution is contradicted by the source: the Leelavati Prize is awarded by the International Mathematical Union at the ICM. Cambridge celebrated the award; it did not confer it. 'Cambridge recognized her ... with the 2026 Leelavati Prize' misattributes the honor.
facts.artifactExcerpt: Cambridge recognized her public communication with the 2026 Leelavati Prize.
facts.sourceExcerpt: The Leelavati Prize, recognising outstanding contributions to increasing the public awareness of mathematics, is awarded every 4 years by the International Mathematical Union (IMU), and is announced at the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM).

facts.reason: The prize citation quoted by Cambridge directly supports Fry's contribution as translating mathematics into public relevance with originality, which grounds the artifact's opening contribution claim; the artifact's narrowing to 'automated decisions' is anchored by the Hello World evidence in C1–C2.
facts.artifactExcerpt: Fry’s contribution is making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.
facts.sourceExcerpt: she has used outstanding creativity and originality to translate mathematics into a language of wonder and relevance for the public without diminishing its scope and importance

facts.reason: Penguin's copy frames the book as examining 'whether they really are an improvement on the humans they are replacing,' which supports the artifact's even-handed 'not automatically fairer' framing — but again only as publisher copy, so it is qualified rather than fully supported.
facts.artifactExcerpt: The point is not that one is automatically fairer.
facts.sourceExcerpt: examines whether they really are an improvement on the humans they are replacing

transfer.scenario: A reader's bank uses an automated system to approve or decline personal loan applications. She is declined with no explanation and wonders whether the decision was fair and what she can do.
transfer.question: Do the profile's closing questions — What is it optimizing? What does it miss? Who carries the consequence? — give this reader real purchase on a system the profile never mentions?
transfer.answer: Yes. 'What is it optimizing?' surfaces that the system likely minimizes lender default risk, not applicant fairness. 'What does it miss?' prompts her to identify unrecorded context — a recent raise, a thin-but-clean credit file, income the data source doesn't capture. 'Who carries the consequence?' clarifies that she, not the bank's model, bears the declined loan, which motivates asking for the decision basis, correcting the record, or requesting human review.
transfer.assessment: The entry point transfers cleanly to a new consequential automated decision without any Fry-specific or Hello World-specific knowledge, so the profile's tool is genuinely reusable rather than decorative. The transfer test passes.

issues.finding: Award misattribution contradicted by the cited source: the Leelavati Prize is awarded by the International Mathematical Union at the International Congress of Mathematicians. Cambridge celebrated the win but did not confer the prize, so 'Cambridge recognized her ... with the 2026 Leelavati Prize' states a false conferral in a factual public card.
issues.artifactExcerpt: Cambridge recognized her public communication with the 2026 Leelavati Prize.

issues.finding: The sentence 'Each can fail differently' generalizes slightly beyond the Penguin copy, which contrasts consistency versus human judgment rather than explicitly stating symmetric failure modes; the inference is reasonable but rests on publisher copy alone.
issues.artifactExcerpt: Each can fail differently, and those differences matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices.

learningDisposition.rationale: The defect is a generalizable pattern worth registering: attributing an award to the institution that celebrates or hosts the announcement rather than to the body that confers it (here Cambridge vs. the International Mathematical Union). Profile makers routinely source award news from an employer's congratulatory page, so a standing check — 'who confers this honor, per the source's own text?' — would catch this class of error across future LUMINAiRY cards. It is not merely a candidate-specific repair.

judgment.summary: The candidate About is craft-strong and nearly publishable: it replaces the rejected title-only incumbent with a genuine contribution claim, one accurate Hello World example, a reader-borne consequence, and three closing questions that demonstrably transfer to new automated-decision scenarios (verified against a loan-approval case). All locked fields — role, lesson, image, seven links, freshness — are preserved byte-for-byte, the 100-word About fits the card, and the voice avoids founder-speak, jargon, award-listing, and inspirational padding. However, one factual claim is contradicted by its own cited source: the Leelavati Prize is awarded by the International Mathematical Union at the ICM, not by Cambridge, so 'Cambridge recognized her public communication with the 2026 Leelavati Prize' misattributes the conferral. Under the standard that PASS requires zero material issues and unsupported/contradicted claims are rejection triggers, the candidate is REJECTED; the fix is a one-sentence attribution correction, and the defect pattern (celebrating institution mistaken for conferring body) should be registered as reusable. The incumbent negative control independently earns REJECT as title-only biography with no contribution, example, consequence, or entry point.

limitations: AI editorial assessment; no observed human comprehension is claimed.
Penguin is publisher copy. It supports the book example and scope, not independent evaluation.
This review does not sign, integrate or publish the profile.
